0.title: Familiar Words, an Unfamiliar World
0.essay:
Most Christians begin reading the Bible in the New Testament, and for good reason: here is Jesus. Yet many soon find that the New Testament has puzzles of its own. Who were the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and why are they always arguing with him? Why are there four Gospels, and why do they not always tell a story in the same words? What did Jesus mean by his parables? Should our church be doing everything the church did in Acts? Must women cover their heads? And what is happening in Revelation?

Who this study is for

It is for the new believer who has started on Matthew and keeps meeting names and customs nobody has explained. It is for the long-time Christian who loves the Gospels but has quietly avoided Revelation, and for the home-group leader who was asked about head coverings and did not know where to begin. You need no Greek. The New Testament was written in the everyday Greek of the marketplace, to be read aloud to congregations of slaves, traders, soldiers and households. God meant ordinary people to understand it. But it was written in a world two thousand years away, and a little knowledge of that world, and of the kinds of writing in front of us, opens it wonderfully.

Four steps

Each unit takes four steps. First, what it is: the world behind the text, or the kind of writing we are reading, explained plainly. Second, how to read it well, worked out on real passages. Third, how it shows Christ, because the whole New Testament is a witness to him. Fourth, what it means for us today.

This study is the companion to Reading the Old Testament Well, which deals with the tabernacle, the sacrifices, the feasts, Israel’s law and the kinds of writing in the Old Testament. We do not repeat that ground; we point to it. Other studies stand alongside this one: Hermeneutics sets out the principles of interpretation, The Bible Book by Book introduces every book, and How We Got Our Bible tells how the New Testament was written, gathered and handed down. Here we stay with the places where readers stumble, and we try to show that every one of them, rightly understood, leads to Christ.

The chapters

From Malachi to John the Baptist; Jesus’ World: Parties, Rulers and Customs; Why Four Gospels?; Parables: The King and His Kingdom; Miracles as Signs; Acts: What to Copy and What Is Simply Reported; Reading the Letters: Someone Else’s Mail; Lasting Principle and Local Custom; Revelation and the Language of Visions; and How the New Testament Reads the Old.

For reflection

Which part of the New Testament have you found hardest to understand, and why? Has anyone ever asked you a question about the New Testament that you could not answer? What would you most like to understand by the end of this study?

1.title: From Malachi to John the Baptist
1.essay:
Turn the page from Malachi to Matthew and you cross about four hundred years in a single breath. The Old Testament closes with a promise: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes” (Malachi 4:5). The New Testament opens in a different world: Romans in charge, a king called Herod, Pharisees and Sadducees, a synagogue in every town, and people speaking Greek. What happened in between?

Persians, Greeks and a common language

Malachi spoke around 430 BC, when Judea was a small province of the Persian Empire. Then, in the 330s BC, Alexander the Great conquered the whole Persian Empire in a few years. When he died in 323 BC his generals divided his conquests, and Judea was ruled first from Egypt by the Ptolemies and then, from 198 BC, from Syria by the Seleucids.

Alexander’s lasting legacy was his language. Greek became the common tongue from Egypt to the borders of India, which is why the New Testament was written in Greek. Many Jews now lived outside the land, scattered through the cities of the empire. In Alexandria, from the third century BC, Jewish scholars translated the Law of Moses into Greek, and the rest of the Old Testament followed over the next century or more. Tradition said seventy translators did the work, so it is called the Septuagint, from the Latin for seventy. It became the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and then of the first Christians, and the apostles often quote it.

The Maccabees and Hanukkah

The great crisis came under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, who called himself Epiphanes, “God made manifest”. In 167 BC he banned circumcision, the Sabbath and the reading of the Law, set up an altar to the Greek god Zeus in the temple, and ordered pigs to be sacrificed. Daniel had foreseen it: forces that would “profane the temple and fortress” and “set up the abomination that makes desolate” (Daniel 11:31).

An old priest named Mattathias refused to sacrifice to the king’s gods and fled to the hills with his five sons. His son Judas, nicknamed Maccabeus, probably meaning “the hammer”, led a guerrilla war, and in 164 BC the Jews retook Jerusalem, cleansed the temple and dedicated a new altar with eight days of rejoicing. That festival, the Feast of Dedication, or Hanukkah, is still kept by Jews today. The story is told in 1 and 2 Maccabees, valuable history though not Scripture (How We Got Our Bible explains why).

Judas’s family, the Hasmoneans, ruled as priests and kings for about a century, but independence did not bring godliness. Devout Jews divided over how to respond, and the parties we meet in the Gospels took shape in those years (Unit 2 introduces them).

Rome arrives

In 63 BC the Roman general Pompey took Jerusalem and walked into the Most Holy Place, to the horror of the Jews. From then on Rome ruled, sometimes through governors and sometimes through local kings. The most famous was Herod the Great, made king of Judea by the Roman senate in 40 BC. He rebuilt the temple on a magnificent scale, and he had a wife and three of his own sons put to death. It fits him all too well that he ordered the killing of the boys of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16).

The synagogue and the waiting

Two things kept faith alive. One was the synagogue, a local meeting place for prayer, the reading of Scripture and teaching. It probably began in the exile, and by Jesus’ day there was one in every Jewish town and in Jewish communities across the empire: “For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues” (Acts 15:21). Jesus preached in them, and Paul began in them wherever he went.

The other was hope. No prophet had spoken since Malachi. Yet the promises stood, and people waited for God to act. They did not all wait for the same thing. Many longed for a son of David who would drive out the Gentiles and rule in righteousness; a Jewish book of the first century BC, the Psalms of Solomon, prays for exactly that. Others looked for Elijah, or for “the Prophet” like Moses (John 1:21). A Samaritan woman said, “I know that Messiah is coming” (John 4:25). And quietly, in the temple, an old man named Simeon was “waiting for the consolation of Israel” (Luke 2:25).

Why it matters for reading

Knowing this world explains a great deal. It is why the crowds wanted to “take him by force to make him king” (John 6:15), and why Jesus withdrew: the title Christ had become full of swords and armies. It is why John the Baptist caused such a stir. Here at last was a prophet, dressed like Elijah (Mark 1:6; 2 Kings 1:8), and “the people were in expectation” (Luke 3:15).

It also lights up a small verse in John: “At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon” (John 10:22–23). It was Hanukkah, the feast remembering the day the temple was cleansed and given back to God. There, at that feast, Jesus spoke of himself as the one “whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world” (John 10:36). The Maccabees had rededicated a building. Walking in its courts was the one the Father had set apart from eternity, the true temple, in whom God would live among his people (John 2:19–21).

A man reading John stopped at “the Feast of Dedication” and looked it up. When he mentioned to a Jewish colleague that Jesus was in the temple at Hanukkah, she was astonished, and it was the first of many conversations.

The fullness of time

Paul looks back over these centuries and sees a hand at work: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Galatians 4:4–5). The silent years were not empty. God had spread one language across the world, planted synagogues and Greek Scriptures in its cities, and let Rome build the roads and keep the rough peace along which the gospel would run. He let hope ripen, and he let every human answer fail: the Maccabean sword, the Hasmonean throne, the Roman peace. Then, when the world had learned that it could not save itself, the Son came, not a day too early and not a day too late.

For reflection

What does it tell you about God that he worked through four centuries in which no prophet spoke? Which of the hopes people had for the Messiah do you recognise in yourself? How does the Feast of Dedication help you see who Jesus is? Where in your own life might God be preparing “the fullness of time” while he seems silent?

2.title: Jesus’ World: Parties, Rulers and Customs
2.essay:
Open almost any page of the Gospels and you meet people the first readers knew at once: Pharisees and Sadducees, scribes, tax collectors, Samaritans, Herod and Pilate. To us they can be names on a page. Yet much of what Jesus said lands with its full force only when we know who was listening, and what his hearers took for granted about honour, purity and meals.

Who was who

Each of these groups has its own entry in this commentary’s Bible World pages, so here we say only why each matters for reading the Gospels.

The Pharisees were a respected movement of devout laymen, devoted to God’s law and to the “tradition of the elders” built around it (Mark 7:3). When people thought of a truly godly man, they thought of a Pharisee. That is why Jesus’ words were so startling: “unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:20). The scribes were the experts in the law, many of them Pharisees. When Jesus taught “as one who had authority, and not as the scribes” (Mark 1:22), the crowds were comparing him with the best Bible teachers they knew.

The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who ran the temple, and they denied the resurrection. So when they tried to make the resurrection look absurd, Jesus answered them from Exodus, from “the book of Moses” that they honoured above all (Mark 12:26). The Essenes, never named in the New Testament, withdrew from a corrupt temple to live in strict purity; the Dead Sea Scrolls probably come from people like them.

The Zealots were ready to fight Rome for God, and the tax collectors collected Rome’s money and were despised as traitors and cheats. Now read the list of the Twelve: “Matthew the tax collector … Simon the Zealot” (Matthew 10:3–4). In any other company those two men might have come to blows. Around Jesus they became brothers.

The Herodians supported Herod’s family, and so, indirectly, Rome. The Pharisees despised them, yet the two joined forces against Jesus (Mark 3:6). Knowing this makes sense of the question about taxes: “Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?” (Mark 12:14). If he said yes, the crowds would see a collaborator. If he said no, the Herodians would report him to Rome. His answer escaped the trap and went deeper than either side: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Mark 12:17). The coin bore Caesar’s image; we bear God’s.

The Samaritans, with their rival temple on Mount Gerizim, were hated by most Jews, and the feeling was returned: “For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans” (John 4:9). Every time a Samaritan turns up in the Gospels as the hero, the first hearers would have flinched.

Rome, the Herods and Pilate

Herod the Great died soon after Jesus was born. His son Herod Antipas ruled Galilee through Jesus’ ministry; Jesus called him “that fox” (Luke 13:32), and he beheaded John the Baptist. (Several different Herods appear in the New Testament; Bible World has a guide to the Herod family.) Judea, with Jerusalem, was ruled by Roman governors, of whom Pontius Pilate was one. The Jewish council could not carry out a death sentence (John 18:31). That is why Jesus was handed to Pilate and died the Roman way, by crucifixion, and why the cry “you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19:12) frightened a governor who owed everything to the emperor.

Honour and shame

In Jesus’ world, honour, your standing in the eyes of others, mattered more than money, and shame was a kind of social death. Guests watched who sat where at a feast (Luke 14:7–11). Read Luke 7:36–50 with this in mind. Simon the Pharisee invited Jesus to dinner and then left out the ordinary courtesies: no water for his feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for his head (Luke 7:44–46). It was a deliberate snub. Then a woman known as “a sinner” came in and wept over Jesus’ feet. Everyone at the table expected him to recoil. Instead he turned to her and honoured her before them all, and said, “Your sins are forgiven” (Luke 7:48).

Crucifixion was designed to shame: a man stripped, lifted up and mocked in public. Jesus “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2). He who had the highest honour in heaven took the lowest place on earth, so that people covered in shame could be welcomed as sons and daughters.

Purity and meals

Israel’s laws of clean and unclean (explained in the companion study Reading the Old Testament Well) shaped daily life. To touch a leper, a corpse or a woman with a flow of blood made you unclean. So when the woman who had bled for twelve years “touched his garment” (Mark 5:27), she should have made him unclean. Instead his cleanness flowed into her. When Jesus “stretched out his hand and touched” a leper (Luke 5:13), the touch did not defile Jesus. It healed the leper.

Meals meant acceptance. To share a table with someone was to say, “You belong with me.” That is why Jesus’ meals caused such offence: “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2). His critics meant it as an accusation. It is the gospel in eight words.

A home group read Luke 7 and could not see why Simon’s missing towel mattered. When the leader explained the courtesies a host owed his guests, someone said quietly, “So Jesus let himself be insulted, and then gave his honour to her.” The room went still.

The King in a real world

Jesus did not come to an idea of humanity but to a real place, among real parties, under a real governor. He walked into its quarrels and took its shame and its uncleanness on himself. He “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12), the unclean place of shame, so that the unclean and the ashamed could be brought in.

For reflection

Which of the groups in Jesus’ world do you find yourself most like? How does knowing about the Herodians change the way you read the question about taxes? Where do you look for honour, and what does it mean that Jesus bore your shame? Who might be surprised to be welcomed at your table?

3.title: Why Four Gospels?
3.essay:
Why does the Bible tell the story of Jesus four times? Would one complete account not be simpler? Around AD 170 a Christian named Tatian thought so, and he wove the four into one continuous story, called the Diatessaron, “through four”. It was popular for a time, especially in Syria. But the church kept the four Gospels side by side, and it was right to.

What a Gospel is

“Gospel” means good news: in the Greek world, the kind of news a runner brought from a battlefield when the war was won. The four Gospels are that news written down. They are true history, gathered from eyewitnesses. Luke says that he “followed all things closely” and drew on those “who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word” (Luke 1:2–3). They look in some ways like the ancient “lives” of famous men, but no ancient life spends a third of its pages on one week and its subject’s death.

And they are history told with a purpose: “these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31). Some people assume that a writer who wants you to believe cannot be trusted. But a witness in court also wants you to believe him. What matters is whether he is telling the truth, and the Gospel writers stake everything on it: “we did not follow cleverly devised myths” (2 Peter 1:16).

Four portraits of one face

Matthew, the former tax collector, wrote chiefly for Jewish believers. He shows Jesus as the King, the son of David, who fulfils the Law and the Prophets. Mark, drawing on Peter’s preaching, wrote probably for the church in Rome, and moves at a run; his Jesus is the Son of God who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Luke, the doctor and careful historian, wrote for Theophilus and the wider Greek world, and shows the Saviour who seeks the lost. John, the beloved disciple, wrote last, and begins before creation with the Word who became flesh. (The Bible Book by Book introduces each in more detail.)

Irenaeus, around AD 180, argued that there could be neither more nor fewer than four Gospels, just as there are four winds. His argument sounds strange to us, but his instinct was sound. Four witnesses, each with his own angle and his own first readers, give us a fuller and surer picture than one could.

Why the accounts differ

Read the Gospels side by side and you will notice differences. They have honest causes.

Selection. No writer told everything. John says that if everything were written, “the world itself could not contain the books” (John 21:25). Each chose what served his purpose.

Order. Ancient writers often grouped events by theme rather than strict sequence. Matthew has the temptation at the temple second and the kingdoms of the world last (Matthew 4:5–10); Luke reverses them (Luke 4:5–12). But Luke simply joins the scenes with “and”, making no claim about order, and ends at Jerusalem because Jerusalem is where his whole Gospel is heading.

Paraphrase. Jesus mostly spoke Aramaic, and the Gospels are written in Greek, so nearly every saying we have is already a faithful translation. Writers gave the sense in their own words. At Jesus’ baptism Matthew has the Father say, “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17), and Mark, “You are my beloved Son” (Mark 1:11). The meaning is identical.

Compression. In Matthew a centurion comes to Jesus himself (Matthew 8:5); in Luke he sends Jewish elders and then friends (Luke 7:3, 6). We still say a king built a palace when his workmen built it; what a man does through his messengers is counted as his. Matthew gives the centurion’s own words and leaves out how they were carried; Luke keeps the messengers.

Eyewitness variety. Matthew and Mark mention one angel at the tomb; Luke and John mention two. Whoever reports one has not denied the second; he simply speaks of the one who spoke. Or take the charge nailed above the cross. Matthew gives “This is Jesus, the King of the Jews” (Matthew 27:37); Mark, “The King of the Jews” (Mark 15:26); Luke, “This is the King of the Jews” (Luke 23:38); John, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews” (John 19:19), and adds that it was written in three languages (John 19:20). Each gives its substance, and all four agree on the point: he died as the King.

Neither forcing nor panic

Faithful Christians have handled these differences in two unhelpful ways. Some force them. One sixteenth-century harmoniser, Andreas Osiander, concluded that Peter must have denied Jesus six times, to keep every detail in a single sequence. Others panic, and decide the Gospels cannot be trusted. Both forget how real testimony works. When four witnesses tell an accident in exactly the same words, a judge suspects they have agreed a story. Agreement in substance with variety in detail is the mark of independent, honest witnesses.

This commentary holds that Scripture as first given is without error in all it affirms. The Gospel writers affirm what happened and what was said. They do not claim to give a recording of every word or a timetable of every hour, and we should not judge them by standards they never claimed. Where a difference still puzzles us, patience is wiser than either forcing or panic; many “contradictions” confidently announced in the past have dissolved on careful reading.

A student was told by a classmate that the Gospels contradict each other about the inscription on the cross. She went home and read all four. She came back saying, “They are like four friends describing the same sign. Not one of them got the point wrong.”

One Lord

Imagine four painters standing around a mountain at dawn, each painting the side he can see. Lay the canvases side by side and you know the mountain better than any single painting could show it. So with the Gospels. Matthew’s King, Mark’s Servant, Luke’s Saviour and John’s eternal Word are not four Jesuses but one, so great that it took four witnesses to show him. Every one of them runs to the same place: a cross outside Jerusalem and an empty tomb. And every one of them is written for the same reason: “that you may believe” (John 20:31).

For reflection

Which Gospel do you know best, and which least? Why might God have given us four Gospels rather than one? How would you answer someone who said the differences prove the Gospels unreliable? What does each Gospel writer help you see in Jesus that the others might not?

4.title: Parables: The King and His Kingdom
4.essay:
“He did not speak to them without a parable” (Mark 4:34). Seeds and soil, sheep and coins, debts and wedding feasts: Jesus taught much of his deepest truth in stories that a child can follow and a scholar cannot exhaust. They are among the best-loved passages in the Bible, and among the most often misread.

What a parable is

The Greek word means something “thrown alongside”: a picture from ordinary life set beside the kingdom of God so that one throws light on the other. Behind it stands the Hebrew word for a comparison, a proverb or a riddle. A parable may be a single sentence, such as “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field” (Matthew 13:44), or a full story. Most have a twist that the first hearers did not expect: a Samaritan hero, a father who runs, a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one.

Parables usually drive home one main point, or a few closely joined points, often carried by the main characters. They are not codes in which every detail stands for something. Ask first: what question or situation prompted this story, and what would its first hearers have felt when it ended?

Why Jesus taught in parables

When the disciples asked about the parables, Jesus gave a hard answer: “To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven” (Mark 4:11–12). He was quoting Isaiah 6. Parables reveal and conceal at the same time. Think of a stained-glass window: from the street it looks dull and grey; step inside and the light pours through. To those who come close and ask, the parables open. To those who have set their hearts against him, they become stories heard and not taken in, which is itself a judgment. Yet even this was mercy, for “he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it” (Mark 4:33), and the door stayed open.

How much is allegory?

Some parables do carry meaning in their details, because Jesus says so. In the parable of the sower he explains, “The sower sows the word” (Mark 4:14), and goes on to the path, the rock and the thorns. In the parable of the weeds he names the sower, the field, the enemy and the harvest (Matthew 13:37–39). So we must not say that parables never have more than one point.

But where Jesus does not explain a detail, we should be slow to explain it for him. Augustine, much as we owe him, read the good Samaritan so that the inn was the church and the innkeeper the apostle Paul (the study Hermeneutics tells the story). A simple rule helps. Details that the story needs in order to work are usually scenery. Details that Jesus, the context or the rest of Scripture explains carry meaning. The rest we hold lightly.

Three worked examples

The sower (Mark 4:3–20). A farmer scatters seed by hand, and it falls on a beaten path, on thin soil over rock, among thorns and on good ground. Much of the seed seems wasted, yet the kingdom is not failing. The word is sown generously, the soil makes the difference, and the harvest from the good soil is astonishing: “thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold” (Mark 4:8). The parable ends with a question for every hearer: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Mark 4:9). What kind of soil am I?

The good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37). A lawyer, “desiring to justify himself”, asked, “And who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29). He wanted to know where his duty stopped. Jesus told of a man beaten and left half dead, passed by a priest and a Levite, the very men whose work was the worship of God. Then came the hero no Jew wanted: a Samaritan. Notice how Jesus turns the question. The lawyer asked whom he must love. Jesus asked, “Which of these three … proved to be a neighbor?” (Luke 10:36). The answer came through gritted teeth, “The one who showed him mercy”, and Jesus said, “You go, and do likewise” (Luke 10:37). That is the main point: love has no boundary, not even an enemy’s face. Many Christians also see in the Samaritan a picture of Christ, the despised outsider who stopped for us and paid for our care. That fits the gospel, but it is an application, not the parable’s own point, and it must never blunt the command.

The two lost sons (Luke 15:11–32). Begin with the setting: tax collectors and sinners were gathering round Jesus, and the Pharisees grumbled (Luke 15:1–2). Jesus answered with three stories of lost things, and the third has two sons. The younger asks for his inheritance, which was like wishing his father dead, wastes it, and ends up feeding pigs. He comes home rehearsing a speech. But “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). In that world a dignified father did not run. He gathered up his robes and shamed himself in the street, so that his son would not be shamed. Then comes the older son, who “was angry and refused to go in” (Luke 15:28). He had obeyed every command and never understood his father’s heart. The story ends with the father pleading and the son outside, and we are never told whether he went in. The Pharisees listening had to finish it themselves.

Timothy Keller often pointed out that there are two lost sons in this story, one lost through his badness and one through his goodness, and that the story leaves us longing for a true elder brother: one who would go to the far country at his own cost to bring his brother home. That brother was the one telling the story.

The King at the centre

The parables are about the kingdom, and a kingdom has a King. Who sows the word? Who owns the field where the treasure lies? Who is the shepherd who carries the lost sheep home on his shoulders? In one parable Jesus put himself in the story outright. The owner of a vineyard sent servant after servant to his tenants, and they were beaten and killed. “He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them” (Mark 12:6). The chief priests understood that the story was about them (Matthew 21:45), and within days they did what the tenants did. The parables of Jesus are, in the end, parables about Jesus.

A woman had always heard the prodigal son preached as a story about rebellious young people. Reading it in its setting, she realised that she was the older brother: dutiful, resentful and far from the Father’s joy.

For reflection

Why do you think Jesus chose stories rather than lectures for so much of his teaching? What question was the good Samaritan answering, and how did Jesus turn it round? Are you more like the younger son or the older one? Where do you see the King himself in the parables you know best?

5.title: Miracles as Signs
5.essay:
Water turned into wine at a village wedding. Five thousand people fed from a boy’s lunch. A man four days dead walking out of his tomb. The Gospels are full of miracles, and modern readers ask two questions at once: did these things really happen, and what were they for?

What miracles are, and are not

Peter used three words on the day of Pentecost: Jesus was “attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs” (Acts 2:22). Mighty works speaks of God’s power, wonders of the astonishment they caused, and signs of their purpose: they point beyond themselves.

They were not magic. Jesus used no spells, and he would not perform on demand. When scribes and Pharisees asked for a sign, he refused (Matthew 12:38–39). Herod “was hoping to see some sign done by him”, and Jesus gave him not even a word (Luke 23:8–9). Nor were miracles meant to compel belief: “Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him” (John 12:37). A sign is like a signpost. You can admire the signpost and never take the road.

John’s seven signs

John chose seven signs and built his Gospel around them: water into wine (John 2), the official’s son healed at a distance (John 4), the man by the pool who had been ill for thirty-eight years (John 5), the feeding of the five thousand and the walking on the sea (John 6), the man born blind (John 9), and Lazarus raised (John 11). The first, he says, “manifested his glory” (John 2:11). Each sign is joined to words that explain it. He feeds the crowd and says, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). He opens blind eyes and says, “I am the light of the world” (John 9:5). He stands at the grave of Lazarus and says, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). The crowd who ate the loaves wanted more bread, not the giver (John 6:26). John wants us to read the signpost and follow it to the one it names.

Previews of the new creation

When John the Baptist, in prison, began to wonder whether Jesus really was the one, Jesus sent back a list: “the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them” (Matthew 11:5). It is Isaiah’s picture of the day when God comes to save: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped” (Isaiah 35:5). The miracles were that day breaking in early.

Notice what kind of miracles Jesus did. No showy marvels, no punishing of enemies. He restored: sight to eyes, strength to legs, sanity to minds, children to parents. His miracles were not interruptions of a healthy world but repairs to a broken one. Every healing was a small preview of the world to come, where “death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore” (Revelation 21:4).

Pointers to who he is

The miracles also asked a question. After the storm on the lake obeyed his word, the terrified disciples said, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). Every Jew knew that it is the LORD who “made the storm be still” (Psalm 107:29). When Jesus told a paralysed man that his sins were forgiven, the scribes rightly asked, “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:7). So Jesus healed him, “that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” (Mark 2:10). The visible miracle vouched for the invisible one.

Taking the objections seriously

Many thoughtful people find miracles impossible to believe. The philosopher David Hume argued in the eighteenth century that our uniform experience of nature will always outweigh anyone’s report of a miracle. The objection deserves a real answer. A law of nature describes what happens when nothing from outside acts; it cannot tell us that nothing ever will, and if God made the world, he is not a prisoner inside it. And to say that experience is uniformly against miracles assumes the very thing in question; the first disciples claimed precisely the experience Hume ruled out.

Nor were they gullible. They knew as well as we do that dead men stay dead; that is why Thomas would not believe without touching the wounds. Christianity does not hide from the question but stakes everything on one miracle: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). That is a claim that can be examined, and the study Apologetics examines it. Believing in miracles does not mean believing every claim of one.

Do such gifts continue?

Here faithful Christians differ. Continuationists, among them respected scholars such as Wayne Grudem and D.A. Carson, hold that all the gifts of the New Testament, healing and miracles included, continue today. They point out that Paul tells the church to “earnestly desire the spiritual gifts” (1 Corinthians 14:1), that no verse says plainly that the gifts will stop, and that “when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away” (1 Corinthians 13:10) most naturally refers to Christ’s return.

Cessationists hold that the gifts that gave new revelation and confirmed the apostles’ message belonged to the church’s foundation. They note that Hebrews speaks of the gospel “attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders” (Hebrews 2:3–4), as something already given, and that Paul calls such works “the signs of a true apostle” (2 Corinthians 12:12). Even in Acts the miracles cluster around the apostles and those close to them.

This commentary’s view: the cessationist view best fits the New Testament’s own shape, and it is held charitably. It does not rest on 1 Corinthians 13:10, which most likely does refer to Christ’s return; it rests on the once-for-all foundation of apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20). That does not mean God has changed. He still heals in answer to prayer, and the church is told to pray for the sick (James 5:14–15). But healing is not guaranteed in this life, and no one today can heal at will. Believers who hold the continuationist view are brothers and sisters, many of them deeply godly. (The Holy Spirit discusses the gifts more fully.)

A man prayed for months for a friend with cancer, and his friend died. He wondered whether his faith had failed. His pastor sat with him over the story of Lazarus, and pointed out that even Lazarus would one day die again. Every healing in the Gospels was a promise, not the final cure. The final cure is resurrection, and his friend’s is still to come.

For reflection

Which of Jesus’ miracles means most to you, and what does it show about him? Why do you think Jesus refused to perform signs on demand? How would you answer a friend who said miracles are impossible? How does seeing the miracles as previews of the new creation help you pray for the sick, and wait?

6.title: Acts: What to Copy and What Is Simply Reported
6.essay:
“Our church should be more like the church in Acts.” Christians often say it, and they usually mean something good: more prayer, more boldness, more love. But which parts of Acts should we copy? Should we cast lots to choose leaders, sell all our property, and expect tongues when people believe?

Description and prescription

Acts is history. It tells us what happened. Some of what it describes is held up for us to follow, some is plainly wrong (Ananias and Sapphira), and some was a one-off event in God’s plan that will never be repeated. Scholars put it like this: a passage may be descriptive, telling what was done, or prescriptive, telling what should be done. A narrative does not become a command simply because it happened.

Four questions help. Does Luke, or the rest of Scripture, approve it? Is it repeated in Acts as a steady pattern? Is it taught plainly in the letters? Or is it tied to a unique moment in the history of salvation?

A book of transition

That last question matters most, because Acts covers about thirty years in which God moved his people from the old covenant to the new. The temple was still standing, and the apostles still went up “at the hour of prayer” (Acts 3:1). The foundation of the church was being laid, and foundations are laid once. And the gospel was crossing one boundary after another, exactly as the risen Lord had said it would: “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). That verse is the outline of the book.

Worked example: the Spirit’s coming

Four times in Acts the Spirit comes in a visible way. At Pentecost he fell on Jewish believers in Jerusalem, and they spoke in other languages (Acts 2:4). In Samaria people believed and were baptised, but the Spirit came only when the apostles Peter and John arrived and laid hands on them (Acts 8:14–17). At the house of the Roman centurion Cornelius the Spirit fell on Gentiles while Peter was still preaching, before anyone was baptised (Acts 10:44–48). In Ephesus about twelve disciples of John the Baptist, who had not heard that the Spirit had been given, were baptised in Jesus’ name, Paul laid his hands on them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied (Acts 19:1–7).

Look at the order. The Spirit comes after baptism, before baptism, with the laying on of hands, without it. If Luke meant to give a formula for every believer, he gave four different ones. What is consistent is the boundary each time: Jews, then Samaritans, whom the Jews despised, then Gentiles, then the last followers of the old era of John the Baptist. Each time God showed publicly that these people were in, on equal terms. Peter drew exactly that lesson: God gave them “the same gift … as he gave to us” (Acts 11:17), and “made no distinction between us and them” (Acts 15:9). In Samaria the delay meant the old feud could not produce two churches: the apostles from Jerusalem saw the Spirit given and welcomed the Samaritans as brothers.

Christians differ here. Pentecostal and charismatic teaching often reads Acts 8 and 19 as a pattern: conversion first, then a later baptism in the Spirit, usually shown by tongues, giving power for service. Many who hold it are earnest and fruitful believers. Others hold that every believer is baptised in the Spirit at conversion, since Paul tells a very mixed church, “in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13), and that we are then filled again and again. This commentary’s view: Pentecost was unique and unrepeatable, as the cross and the resurrection are, and the delays in Acts 8 and 19 mark the gospel crossing new boundaries, not a pattern for every believer; every Christian is baptised in the Spirit at conversion and should seek to be filled with him continually. (The Holy Spirit discusses this further.)

Worked examples: possessions, lots and handkerchiefs

The first believers “had all things in common” (Acts 2:44), and owners of land sold it for the needy (Acts 4:34–35). Was this a compulsory system? Peter’s words to Ananias answer: “While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?” (Acts 5:4). Ananias’s sin was lying, not keeping property. Believers still had homes; the church met in them (Acts 2:46; 12:12). What Acts holds up is not a scheme but a spirit, glad and costly generosity, which the letters command too (1 John 3:17).

The apostles chose Matthias to replace Judas by casting lots (Acts 1:26). That happened before Pentecost, and lots are never used again in the New Testament. Once the Spirit had come, the church chose leaders by prayer, Scripture and spiritual wisdom (Acts 6:3; 14:23).

People laid the sick in the street so that Peter’s shadow might fall on them (Acts 5:15), and handkerchiefs that had touched Paul were carried to the sick (Acts 19:12). Luke calls these “extraordinary miracles” (Acts 19:11). They were God bearing witness to his apostles, not techniques to sell in prayer cloths.

What is normative

What, then, should a church copy? The things Acts shows again and again, and the letters teach plainly. “And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42). Those who believe are baptised (Acts 2:41). The church gathers on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7). Elders are appointed (Acts 14:23). The gospel goes out, and believers suffer for it with joy. That is the church in Acts, and any congregation can be like it.

A young pastor came to Acts hungry for miracles and frustrated that his small church saw none. As he read it again with these questions, he saw how much of Acts was the apostles preaching Christ and the church gathering to hear, pray and break bread. He stopped waiting for something else to happen and gave himself to the things Acts repeats.

The risen Lord at work

Luke calls his Gospel an account of “all that Jesus began to do and teach” (Acts 1:1). Acts, then, is what Jesus went on to do, from heaven, by his Spirit, through his people. The hero of the book is not Peter or Paul but the risen Lord. It ends with Paul under guard in Rome, “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance” (Acts 28:31). The chains are on the apostle, not on the word. The book stops, but the story has not ended, and every church that preaches Christ is still living in it.

For reflection

What have you heard people say we should copy from Acts? Which of the four questions do you find most useful, and why? What does the varied order of the four “Pentecosts” teach? Which of the marks of the church in Acts 2:42 most needs strengthening in your own life or church?

7.title: Reading the Letters: Someone Else’s Mail
7.essay:
Twenty-one of the twenty-seven books of the New Testament are letters. Reading them is a little like reading someone else’s mail, or hearing one side of a telephone call. We catch the answers but not the questions. We hear names we do not know. Yet these letters, written to real churches with real troubles, are God’s word to us, and a few simple habits open them up.

What a New Testament letter is

A letter was written on papyrus, often dictated to a secretary. At the end of Romans the secretary adds his own greeting: “I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord” (Romans 16:22). The apostle might take the pen for the last lines: “See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand” (Galatians 6:11). A trusted friend carried it, sometimes hundreds of miles, and it was read aloud to the gathered church (Colossians 4:16). (Bible World describes letters and scrolls in more detail.)

Most were written for an occasion. A report reached Paul of quarrels in Corinth: “it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you” (1 Corinthians 1:11). The Corinthians wrote him questions: “Now concerning the matters about which you wrote” (1 Corinthians 7:1). The Galatians were turning to “a different gospel” (Galatians 1:6). The Philippians sent a gift. These are not essays written in a study; they are pastoral letters written into the middle of church life. That is why they feel so alive. Yet Peter already counted Paul’s letters with “the other Scriptures” (2 Peter 3:16). Written to them, they were written for us too.

Five habits for reading a letter

Read it whole. The first hearers heard the whole letter at a sitting. Philippians takes about fifteen minutes to read aloud. Before you study one verse, read the whole letter through, and notice what keeps coming up.

Rebuild the situation from the letter itself. Ask what had happened, what the readers were asking and what was going wrong. Listen to the one side of the call and work out the other, carefully. Let the letter tell you; do not invent a background and then read the letter through it.

Follow the argument. Letters argue. Watch the small joining words: “therefore”, “for”, “so”, “but”. A verse lifted out of its paragraph loses its “therefore”, and often its meaning.

Notice indicative before imperative. These are grammar words. The indicative tells what is true; the imperative tells us what to do. In the letters, what God has done in Christ comes first, and what we do follows from it. Ephesians spends three chapters on what God has done before it says, “I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called” (Ephesians 4:1). Romans spends eleven before, “I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God” (Romans 12:1). The commands rest on grace. Read them the other way round and the gospel becomes a burden.

Know the shape. Ancient letters had a pattern, and the New Testament letters fill it with Christ: the writer and readers named, a greeting (usually “grace” and “peace”), a thanksgiving or prayer that often previews the letter’s themes, the body, instructions, and closing greetings.

Worked example: Philippians

Let us try it on Philippians. Who wrote it, and to whom? Paul and Timothy, “To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons” (Philippians 1:1). Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, where Paul had planted the church years before; Lydia and the jailer were among its first members (Acts 16).

What had happened? Paul is in prison (Philippians 1:7, 13). The church has sent him a gift by one of its members, Epaphroditus: “having received from Epaphroditus the gifts you sent, a fragrant offering” (Philippians 4:18). Epaphroditus fell ill and nearly died, and now Paul is sending him home with this letter (Philippians 2:25–30). The church faces opponents outside (Philippians 1:28). And there is trouble inside. Near the end Paul names two women: “I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to agree in the Lord” (Philippians 4:2). They had worked side by side with him in the gospel, and now they could not agree.

Now follow the argument. Paul calls the church to live “worthy of the gospel of Christ”, standing firm “in one spirit, with one mind” (Philippians 1:27). He presses it home: “Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves” (Philippians 2:3). Then he gives the reason, and it is not a technique. It is a Person: “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:5–7). He “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8), and God has exalted him, so that “every knee should bow … and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord” (Philippians 2:10–11). Then come examples of that mind in action: Timothy, Epaphroditus, Paul himself. Only after all this does Paul turn to the two women.

Stop and take that in. One of the most glorious passages ever written about Christ, his eternal glory, his descent to a slave’s death, his exaltation over the whole universe, was written in part to help two women in a small church in Macedonia to make peace. Paul did not think a church quarrel too small for the cross, or the cross too lofty for a church quarrel. The Son of God stooping from heaven is the answer to two Christians who will not stoop to each other.

What it means for us

Reading this way protects us from misusing favourite verses. A young man had “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13) printed on his sports kit. When he read it in its paragraph, he saw that Paul was speaking of contentment in hunger and plenty: “I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content” (Philippians 4:11). The verse was not about winning matches but about being content in Christ when you lose. He found it a far stronger promise than the one he had printed.

And this way of reading always brings us back to grace. Every “therefore” in the letters points back to what Christ has done. Read them in order, and the commands come to you as a family’s instructions to its own children, not a stranger’s demands.

For reflection

Which New Testament letter could you read straight through this week? How does knowing about Euodia and Syntyche change the way you read Philippians 2? Can you think of a verse you have used without its context? Where do you find yourself reading the commands without the grace that comes before them?

8.title: Lasting Principle and Local Custom
8.essay:
“Greet one another with a holy kiss” (Romans 16:16). Few churches obey that literally, and few Christians feel guilty about it. But if we can set aside that command, a thoughtful reader may ask, why not others? How do we tell a lasting principle from a local custom without simply keeping the commands we like?

Why the question cannot be avoided

Every part of the New Testament was written to people in a particular culture, and no church today obeys every command in its first-century form. There are two dangers. One is to treat everything inconvenient as “just culture”, until the Bible can say nothing we do not already think. The other is to treat every first-century form as binding, and so lay burdens on consciences that God has not laid.

The key question: what reason does Scripture give?

The surest guide is to ask what reason the text itself gives. When a command is grounded in creation, which comes before every culture, in the gospel, what Christ has done, or in the character of God, it is lasting. Jesus himself settled a question about marriage by going back to creation: “Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female” (Matthew 19:4). When a command is grounded in a local reason, such as what was shameful in that city or what would offend outsiders there, the principle still binds us, but its outward form may change. A second question helps: what did this action mean to them, and what carries that meaning for us?

Worked examples

The holy kiss. The reason behind it is that believers are one family in Christ. What is commanded is the warmth of a family greeting, always pure. Where a kiss carries that meaning it may still be used; where it does not, a handshake or an embrace obeys the command. What is not optional is greeting one another as family.

Food offered to idols. In Corinth most meat in the market had passed through a pagan temple. Paul’s reasons are lasting: an idol is nothing, “the earth is the Lord’s” (1 Corinthians 10:26), yet love limits liberty: “take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak” (1 Corinthians 8:9), and Christians may never share in idol worship (1 Corinthians 10:21). The question is still real where Christians live among temples and shrines, and the principles apply to every “grey area”: freedom bounded by love, no compromise with idols, and “do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Slaves and masters. Paul tells bondservants to serve “as you would Christ”, and masters to stop threatening, “knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven” (Ephesians 6:5, 9). He regulated an institution he did not create (Bible World explains slavery in the ancient world), but he planted principles that undermined it: the same Master over both, a runaway slave to be welcomed back “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16), freedom to be taken where possible (1 Corinthians 7:21), and “enslavers” listed among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). The lasting principle is to serve as to the Lord; the institution was never commanded, and Christians like Wilberforce were right to end it.

Head coverings (1 Corinthians 11:2–16). Paul gives several reasons at once: an order of headship in which even Christ has a head (11:3), creation, “For man was not made from woman, but woman from man” (1 Corinthians 11:8), “the angels” (11:10), what “nature itself” teaches (11:14), what was shameful in Corinth (11:5–6), and the practice of the churches (11:16). Some churches still ask women to cover their heads in worship, because Paul appeals to creation and to all the churches; that view takes his reasons seriously and deserves respect. Most Christians hold that the creation principle remains while the covering was the form it took in Corinth, where a covered head marked a married woman as honourable; they note that Paul says a woman’s hair “is given to her for a covering” (1 Corinthians 11:15). This commentary’s view: the creation principle of male and female and the husband’s headship is permanent; the head covering was its Corinthian form.

Where Christians differ: women’s roles

The hardest case concerns 1 Corinthians 14:34–35 and 1 Timothy 2:11–14: “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet. For Adam was formed first, then Eve” (1 Timothy 2:12–13).

Egalitarians hold that every ministry, the eldership included, is open to men and women alike. They point to Galatians 3:28, “there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus”; to the Spirit poured out so that “your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Acts 2:17); to Phoebe, Priscilla, and Junia, “well known to the apostles” (Romans 16:7). They read 1 Timothy 2 as answering a particular crisis in Ephesus, where false teachers were influencing untaught women, and they argue that just as the church came to see that Paul’s instructions to slaves did not endorse slavery, so his limits on women addressed his own time.

Complementarians hold that men and women are equal in worth and dignity, “heirs with you of the grace of life” (1 Peter 3:7), but given different callings. They note that Galatians 3:28 is about who belongs to Christ, not who holds which office, and that the decisive difference from slavery is the reason Paul gives: slavery is never grounded in creation, but here Paul appeals to the order of creation, before the fall and before any culture. They read 1 Corinthians 14:34–35 alongside 11:5, where women pray and prophesy aloud, and so take it to concern the public weighing of prophecies, which carried teaching authority, rather than total silence.

This commentary’s view: complementarian. Women pray, serve and teach in many settings, some prophesied in apostolic times, and Deborah and Huldah were prophets raised up by God, but the eldership and authoritative teaching in the gathered church belong to qualified men, grounded in creation. The studies Biblical Womanhood and Biblical Manhood set this out more fully, and they insist that a church holding this view should be the first to open every door of service Scripture leaves open.

Christians who love Scripture hold both views. The question should be discussed with humility and charity, without suspecting the motives of those who differ.

A young woman left a Bible study confused by an argument about head coverings. An older friend walked her through the reasons Paul gives, one by one. “I still have questions,” she said, “but now I know which questions to ask.”

The shape of the cross

Look again at the reasons the New Testament gives, and you find Christ at the bottom of them. Husbands are to love their wives “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). The strong bear with the weak, “For Christ did not please himself” (Romans 15:3). Masters treat slaves as men who have the same Master. The lasting principles are not arbitrary rules; they take the shape of the cross, and they are kept by people who know they have been loved like that.

For reflection

Can you think of a command you have set aside as “cultural”? What reason does Scripture give for it? Why does it matter whether a command is grounded in creation or in local custom? How can you hold your convictions about disputed questions firmly and still love those who differ?

9.title: Revelation and the Language of Visions
9.essay:
Many Christians never open Revelation; it seems too strange and too frightening. Others read little else, and treat it as a code for decoding the news. Both miss what the book says about itself. It begins with a blessing: “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it” (Revelation 1:3). God meant it to be read, heard, understood and obeyed.

What kind of writing it is

Its first word, apokalypsis, means “unveiling”. Revelation draws back the curtain on what is really happening in the world. It belongs to a kind of writing called apocalyptic, which Jewish readers knew from Daniel, Ezekiel and Zechariah: visions full of symbols, angels who explain, and history seen from heaven’s point of view, usually given to God’s people under pressure. Revelation is also a prophecy and a letter, written “to the seven churches that are in Asia” (Revelation 1:4), seven real congregations in what is now western Turkey, some of them suffering and some of them comfortable.

Think of a political cartoon. Nobody thinks a giant bear has really crossed a border, yet everybody understands the cartoon, and it often tells the truth more sharply than an article. Revelation works like that. A dragon “with seven heads and ten horns” (Revelation 12:3) is not a creature to picture but a power to recognise: Satan, working in many forms.

Symbols drawn from the Old Testament

Revelation hardly ever quotes the Old Testament formally, yet it echoes it on almost every page. Its beasts rise from the sea as in Daniel, where “four great beasts came up out of the sea” (Daniel 7:3), and Daniel is told that “These four great beasts are four kings” (Daniel 7:17). Its plagues echo the plagues of Egypt. Its final city has a river and the tree of life, as Eden did. And sometimes Revelation explains its own symbols: “the seven lampstands are the seven churches” (Revelation 1:20). So the first rule is to let Scripture explain the pictures, Revelation itself first, then the Old Testament it draws on, not the newspaper.

Numbers that carry meaning

Numbers in Revelation usually speak of meaning rather than quantity. Seven is completeness: seven churches stand for the whole church, and the seven spirits are the Spirit in his fullness. Twelve is the people of God, twelve tribes and twelve apostles. A thousand is a vast, full number. So the 144,000 sealed “from every tribe of the sons of Israel” (Revelation 7:4), twelve times twelve times a thousand, are the whole people of God, complete and safe. John hears that number; then he looks and sees “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation” (Revelation 7:9). What he heard and what he saw are the same people from two sides. Three and a half years, expressed as forty-two months, 1,260 days, or “a time, and times, and half a time” (Revelation 12:14), borrowed from Daniel 7:25, is a broken seven: a limited time of trouble, real but cut short.

Four ways of reading

Faithful Christians read Revelation in four main ways. Preterists see most of it fulfilled in the first century, in Rome and the Jewish war of AD 66–70, taking seriously “the things that must soon take place” (Revelation 1:1). Historicists, including many Reformers, read it as a map of church history, and often saw the papacy in the beast. Futurists place most of chapters 4–22 still ahead, whether as historic premillennialists, who expect the church to pass through a final tribulation before Christ reigns on earth, or as dispensationalists, who add a rapture before a seven-year tribulation. Idealists see pictures of the conflict between Christ and Satan through the whole age. Each stresses something true.

This commentary’s view: it follows the historic Reformed mainstream, amillennial and broadly idealist but anchored in the first century. The book spoke first to seven churches under Rome, then in repeated cycles pictures the conflict of the whole age, ending in Christ’s return. The seals, trumpets and bowls are not a timetable but parallel series, each running from the cross to the end with rising intensity. The thousand years are the present age, in which Christ reigns from heaven and Satan is bound so that he cannot stop the gospel reaching the nations. Then come one return, one resurrection and judgment, and the new creation. (The studies End Times Models and Already and Not Yet explain these views and this age between the comings.)

Read for comfort, not fear

The first readers were under real pressure. In Pergamum a believer named Antipas had been killed (Revelation 2:13). To Smyrna Christ said, “Do not fear what you are about to suffer … Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10). Revelation was given to strengthen frightened Christians, not to frighten strong ones. When John saw the risen Christ he fell at his feet as though dead, “But he laid his right hand on me, saying, ‘Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades’” (Revelation 1:17–18). Whoever holds the keys decides who goes in and who comes out. They are in the hand that was pierced for us.

A teenager had been terrified by an end-times film and lay awake fearing she would be “left behind”. Her pastor did not give her a chart. He read her Revelation 1 and 5, and asked her who was on the throne. She came back the next week having read the whole book, and said the strangest thing about it was how often everyone in it was singing.

The Lamb on the throne

At the heart of the book is a scene in heaven. No one is found worthy to open the scroll of God’s purposes, and John weeps. Then an elder says, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5:5). John turns to see a lion, and sees instead “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6). That is the key to the whole book. The Lion conquers by being the Lamb. Christ’s victory was won on the cross, and his people conquer the same way, “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11).

The beasts rage, the empires boast, Babylon glitters and falls. But the centre of the universe is a throne, and on it is the Lamb. And the book ends with the promise every page has been moving towards: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people” (Revelation 21:3). “They will see his face” (Revelation 22:4). No wonder the church’s last prayer in the Bible is this: “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

For reflection

Have you avoided Revelation, or been fascinated by it for the wrong reasons? How does knowing that it is full of Old Testament pictures change how you read it? Why does it matter that John heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb? What fear in your life needs the words “Fear not, I am the first and the last”?

10.title: How the New Testament Reads the Old
10.essay:
The New Testament quotes the Old hundreds of times and echoes it far more often. Sometimes the way it does so puzzles us. Matthew tells how Joseph took Mary and the child to Egypt and stayed until Herod died, “to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, ‘Out of Egypt I called my son’” (Matthew 2:15). Look up the verse in Hosea and it is not a prediction at all. It looks back to the exodus. Was Matthew careless with his Bible? No. He was reading it the way Jesus taught his disciples to read it.

Quotation, allusion and echo

The New Testament uses the Old in different ways. Sometimes it quotes, often with “it is written” or “to fulfill what the Lord had spoken” (Matthew 1:22). Sometimes it alludes, borrowing a phrase without naming the source. Sometimes there is only an echo, which a reader soaked in the Old Testament would catch. At Jesus’ baptism the voice from heaven says, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). No source is named, but the words echo Psalm 2, where God says to his anointed King, “You are my Son” (Psalm 2:7), and Isaiah 42, “Behold my servant … in whom my soul delights” (Isaiah 42:1). In one sentence the Father names Jesus both the royal Son and the Servant who would suffer.

“Fulfilled” means more than predicted

Some Old Testament passages are straightforward predictions, like Micah’s promise that a ruler would come from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2). But the New Testament word for “fulfil” means to fill something full, and many fulfilments are patterns being filled, not forecasts coming true.

Go back to Hosea. “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 11:1). God had called Israel his son at the exodus: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22). But the next verse in Hosea is sad: “The more they were called, the more they went away” (Hosea 11:2). Israel was a son who failed. Matthew saw that in Jesus God’s Son was living Israel’s story over again, and getting it right. Look at the chapters that follow. Jesus comes out of Egypt. He passes through the waters at his baptism, as Israel passed through the sea. He is led into the wilderness for forty days, as Israel wandered for forty years. He is tested with hunger, and he answers from Deuteronomy, the book of Israel’s wilderness years: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). Where Israel grumbled and fell, he stood. Then he goes up a mountain and teaches God’s law. Matthew is not misusing Hosea. He is showing us that Jesus is the true Israel, the obedient Son.

The same pattern runs through the New Testament. Israel was God’s vine and yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:7); Jesus says, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). Jesus speaks of “something greater than the temple”, “something greater than Jonah”, “something greater than Solomon” (Matthew 12:6–42). God’s people, places and institutions in the Old Testament were sketches, and he is the finished portrait. This is what is called typology, and the companion study Reading the Old Testament Well sets it out, with its careful distinction between links named in the New Testament, links consistent with it, and speculation to avoid. The study Hermeneutics explains it too.

A method learned from Jesus

Where did the apostles learn to read like this? From Jesus himself. On the road to Emmaus, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). That evening he told the apostles “that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled”, and “he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:44–45). He summed it up: “that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations” (Luke 24:46–47). The apostles did not invent a clever method. They were taught it by the risen Lord, in the most wonderful Bible study ever given.

Peter adds that the prophets themselves “searched and inquired carefully” about “the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories” (1 Peter 1:10–11).

Can we read the Old Testament the same way?

Yes, with discipline. We are not apostles and we receive no new revelation, but we may follow the paths the apostles marked. Read every passage first for its plain meaning in its own setting. Then ask where the New Testament takes it: what promise it carries forward, what pattern it shows, what covenant it belongs to, and how it is fulfilled in Christ. Do not hunt for Christ in every peg and colour; trace the great lines of the story to where they meet. The companion study shows how.

A woman had quietly stopped reading the Old Testament, thinking that a Christian had all she needed in the New. Then she noticed how often the New Testament says “as it is written”. She began reading the two together, Exodus with John, Isaiah with the Gospels, and found that the New Testament grew deeper the more of the Old she knew. “It was as if the New Testament had been speaking a language,” she said, “and I had only just learned it.”

The witness to him

Stand back now and see what we have seen. Four centuries of waiting and confused hope found their answer in him. The Pharisees and Sadducees, the Herods and Pilate, all had to decide about him. Four Gospels are four portraits of his one face. The parables are stories of his kingdom, and he is the beloved Son sent last. The miracles are signs pointing to him and previews of the world he will make new. Acts is what he went on doing from heaven. The letters rest every command on what he has done. Revelation opens heaven and shows him, the Lamb who was slain, at the centre of the throne. And the Old Testament, read with the New, turns out to have been speaking of him all along: “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

That is why the New Testament was written. It is not, in the end, a book about the first century, or about how to read ancient letters, or even about the church. It is a witness to a person. John says it for all the writers: “these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31). Read it well, and you will find him. Better still, you will find that he has found you.

For reflection

How does the story of Israel help you understand Jesus’ baptism and temptation? Can you think of another place where the New Testament shows Jesus as “something greater” than an Old Testament person or institution? How can you read the Old Testament with Christ in view without making it say what it does not say? Looking back over this study, where have you seen Christ most clearly?
